newsitem.title: USA: Du Pont lawyers say jury delay unusually long.
newsitem.headline: Du Pont lawyers say jury delay unusually long.

text.p: A lawyer for millionaire murder defendant John du Pont said Monday the jury in the case was taking an unusually long time to reach a verdict after a sixth day of deliberations.
"It is unusual that they're out as long as they are? We think that it is," attorney Taras Wochuck told reporters after the day's deliberations.
Asked whether the defence was seeking a mistrial based on the lengthy deliberations, he said, "I'm not going to comment on that."
Prosecutors said the jurors were still working hard and there were no signs of a hung jury.
"They have not sent out signals indicating that they're tired," Delaware County District Attorney Patrick Meehan said.

"In fact, I really read it the other way. The fact that the jury is working this hard is an indication that they think they're making some progress; they're getting close to something and they just don't want to quit," he said.
Du Pont, a millionaire chemicals heir, is charged with first and third-degree murder as well as voluntary manslaughter in the Jan. 26, 1996 killing of Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz.
Du Pont's lawyers have conceded du Pont killed Schultz, but are seeking a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity.
In addition to verdicts of not guilty or not guilty by reason of insanity, the jurors can render verdicts of guilty or guilty but mentally ill.
Meehan had said Saturday the jurors' questions so far indicated they may have already moved past the issue of insanity and were trying to determine the degree of homicide which applies to the case.
A hung jury and retrial could give du Pont's lawyers a chance to try again with an insanity defence.
But Wochuck indicated the defence was eager for a verdict. "Let's get it over with," he said.
Meehan said Monday if there were a retrial, the intense publicity the case has received could make it difficult to find a suitable jury in the suburban Philadelphia county.
Delaware County Court of Common Pleas Judge Patricia Jenkins told the jury Saturday it was evident they were having difficulty, but the jury itself made no mention of any problems.
Jenkins could at some point urge the jury to redouble its efforts, but Meehan said Monday any such statement would probably require a declaration by the jury that it was deadlocked.

After taking a day of rest Sunday, the jurors began deliberations Monday morning, worked through lunch, and, for the first time, did not appear in the courtroom at all during the day to ask a question or receive an answer to a question posed earlier.
The jury worked Monday with visual aids they requested late Saturday. The six men and six women on the jury were given note pads, markers, an easel board and tape to help them in their deliberations.
